disclaimer: Proxy modeled on the public structure of a Kolbe A Index result (four Action Modes, 1-10 per mode, three zones). Not the licensed instrument; items and labels are original wording.

scale.prompt_suffix: Which one is closest to what you actually do, not what you think you should do?

fact_finder.name: Fact Finder
fact_finder.question: How you gather and share information

sequence_verb.counteract: summarize and clarify the bottom line

do: Give the main points with enough context
Bridge detail people and big-picture people
Ask for the specifics you actually need
dont: Over-research when a summary will do
Get rushed into deciding without data

do: Keep what you use visible and within reach
Deal with tasks as they come
dont: Repeat a pattern just because it's the pattern
Lock into a single way of working
Build elaborate systems you won't keep

do: Finish one thing before starting the next
Sequence the work and protect the sequence

quick_start.name: Quick Start
quick_start.question: How you deal with risk and uncertainty

do: Plan the change before making it
dont: Commit before the risk is clear

do: Improvise when you must, prepare when you can

implementor.name: Implementor
implementor.question: How you handle space and tangibles

sequence_verb.respond: check the materials and fix what's there

do: Describe solutions in words and visuals
dont: Judge a solution only by its physical form

do: Walk through the real space before concluding
dont: Build from scratch what could be repaired

do: Use tools and materials to think
dont: Leave the build to someone else

scoring_notes: Each item has three options tagged with a zone. Per mode: net = (initiate count minus counteract count) / answered; score = round(5.5 + 4.5 * net), clamped 1-10. All-initiate -> 10, all-counteract -> 1, all-respond or balanced -> 6 (respond zone). Label = zone of the final score. Mode confidence = share of answers in the modal zone. Option order is varied per item so position never signals the zone. See scoring.ts.

items.text: You're handed a new project. What do you actually do first?

options.text: Get the gist and move. I'll fill in details later.
Gather enough to be sure it's right, then start.
Dig in. I want the history, the data and the specifics before anything.

items.text: Someone sends you a long report. What do you do with it?

options.text: Read it carefully end to end and take notes.
Read the summary and the parts that apply to me.
Skim it, or ask someone for the bottom line.

items.text: When you explain something to a teammate, how do you do it?

options.text: Short and punchy. The headline, then done.
The main points, with a bit of context.
Thoroughly. Background and reasons, so it's precise.

items.text: You need to decide, and the information is incomplete. What happens?

options.text: I hold off until I've researched it properly.
I decide on a good estimate. Close enough is fine.
I get the key missing pieces, then decide.

items.text: You're buying something expensive, like a camera or a car. How do you go about it?

options.text: Compare specs, read reviews, maybe build a spreadsheet.
Check a couple of trusted sources and go.
Trust my gut and the first good recommendation.

items.text: A friend asks why you believe something. How do you answer?

options.text: I explain my reasoning in a sentence or two.
I walk them through the evidence step by step.
The short version. I don't like justifying at length.

items.text: Picture your desk, or your computer desktop. What does it look like most days?

options.text: Everything has a place and a system.
Mostly tidy, with a few piles.
Organized chaos. I know roughly where things are.

items.text: You start a repeating task, like a weekly report. What do you do?

options.text: Do it differently each time, depending on what's going on.
Build a template or checklist so it runs the same every time.
Follow a loose routine, and change it when needed.

items.text: You're in the middle of a task and get interrupted. How does that land?

options.text: Fine. I switch, and switch back whenever.
A bit annoying, but I handle it and come back.
It throws me. I need to finish what I started.

items.text: How many projects do you like running at once?

options.text: One at a time, done properly, before the next.
Several. I like juggling and jumping between them.
A few, as long as they're reasonably in order.

items.text: A process at work is clunky, but it's the official way. What do you do?

options.text: Follow it mostly, and suggest fixes.
Find a shortcut or work around it.
Follow it, and if it's broken, redesign the whole process.

items.text: How do you plan a trip?

options.text: Detailed itinerary, bookings, backup plans.
Book a flight and wing it.
Key things booked, the rest figured out there.

items.text: You get an idea at ten at night. What happens next?

options.text: I start on it right then.
I write it down and look at it in the morning.
I sit with it a while to see if it's really worth doing.

items.text: A deadline is a week away. When do you really get going?

options.text: Right away, steadily, so there's no rush at the end.
The last day or two. Pressure is where I do my best work.
Somewhere in the middle, with a push at the end.

items.text: Someone proposes a big change to how the team works. Your first reaction?

options.text: Interesting. Let's pilot it on something small.
Why change what works? Show me it's safe first.
Let's try it now and fix it as we go.

items.text: How do you feel about improvising, say, presenting without preparing?

options.text: Love it. I'm better off the cuff.
Okay in a pinch, but I'd rather have notes.
I avoid it. I prepare thoroughly.

items.text: You're stuck on a problem. What's your instinct?

options.text: Stick with the proven approach and work it harder.
Throw out ten possible fixes and try the wildest one.
Try a couple of reasonable options.

items.text: How often do you start things that end up unfinished?

options.text: Rarely. I don't start what I can't see through.
Sometimes.
Constantly. Starting is the fun part.

items.text: You need to explain a concept to someone. What do you reach for?

options.text: Words. I describe it.
A quick sketch or diagram.
A physical thing. A model, a prototype, something they can hold.

items.text: Something breaks at home. What do you do?

options.text: Take it apart and fix it myself.
Call someone or replace it. I'd rather not touch it.
Try a basic fix, then call someone.

items.text: You're designing something new. Where does it live first?

options.text: In sketches and mockups.
In my head, or in a doc. I can picture it fully.
In my hands. I build a rough version right away.

items.text: How much does your physical setup matter to how you work?

options.text: A lot. I need the right tools, gear and space.
Somewhat. Comfortable is enough.
Hardly at all. Give me a laptop anywhere.

items.text: How do you learn a new tool or device?

options.text: Read or watch about it first, then use it.
Pick it up and mess with it until it works.
Try the basics, and look things up when stuck.

items.text: What's your relationship with hands-on work, like building, repairing or crafting?

options.text: I enjoy it now and then.
It's where I feel most alive.
I'd rather think, talk or design than build.
